seo.title: Holding Company & Group Financial Structure | DNH
seo.description: Understand the relationships between resources, liquidity, obligations, ownership and investment priorities across a corporate group.

sections.heading: Holding-company financial structure: see the whole group
paragraphs: Each company may appear financially sound on its own while cash, debt and investment programmes remain uncoordinated across the group.
Drawing on Dr Nasim Mohammadhassani’s analytical perspective, DNH helps clarify financial relationships between companies and the issues that matter for group-level decisions.

sections.heading: When does a group financial structure need review?
sections.intro: As companies, projects and obligations increase, financial decisions become more complex. Resources may sit in one part of a group while another faces liquidity pressure.

items.title: Uneven liquidity
items.description: Some companies hold cash while others face funding needs.

items.title: Fragmented obligations
items.description: The timing of obligations and the resources required to meet them may not be visible in one picture.

items.title: Concurrent investments
items.description: Several projects compete for the group’s limited resources.

items.title: Uncoordinated decisions
items.description: Company priorities may diverge from the needs and financial objectives of the group.

sections.closing: Understanding each company is necessary, but it is not sufficient for group-level decisions.

sections.heading: The financial position of each company is not the whole holding-company picture
sections.intro: Subsidiary performance is only part of the picture. Group decisions require an understanding of how resources, obligations and financial plans interact.

groups.label: GROUP-LEVEL FINANCIAL VIEW
groups.title: Looking across the group
bullets: The group-wide effect of each company’s decisions

sections.closing: The aim is not to replace company financial reporting, but to understand the relationships relevant to group-level decisions.

sections.heading: How are group resources and obligations connected?
paragraphs: A holding-company review needs a comprehensible view of company structure, resource flows and obligations.
That view makes dependencies and areas requiring further work easier to identify.

items.title: Parent company and ownership
items.description: Ownership structure and relationships between group entities.

items.title: Subsidiaries
items.description: The role and financial position of operating units.

items.title: Cash flows
items.description: Sources, uses and possible movement of liquidity between companies.

items.title: Debt and obligations
items.description: Financial commitments and their relationship with group resources.

items.title: Projects and capital allocation
items.description: Capital needs and possible priorities for the use of resources.

sections.note: This is a conceptual view, not a formal consolidated financial statement. Ownership, cash movement and financial obligations are distinct relationships and must not be treated as interchangeable.

sections.heading: Cash held by one company is not always available to the whole group
sections.intro: Profitability and cash are different. Operating needs, obligations or transfer restrictions may prevent one company’s cash from being used elsewhere immediately.

items.title: Accounting profit
items.description: Reported profit does not necessarily mean the same amount of cash has been received or is available.

items.title: Cash available
items.description: Where is cash located, and how much is required by that company’s own operations?

items.title: Transferable liquidity
items.description: Can resources be moved between companies under the applicable financial, contractual and other requirements?

sections.closing: Cash in one company does not in itself mean it can be transferred immediately to another. Location, obligations and usability must be considered together.

sections.heading: Where should the group’s limited capital be prioritised?
paragraphs: Company development, working capital and new projects may all require funding at the same time.
Reviewing financing and allocation options clarifies costs, constraints and possible implications.

items.title: Group financing
items.description: The genuine need for new resources, financing cost and associated obligations.

items.title: Debt and repayment
items.description: Distribution of obligations and their fit with company cash flows.

items.title: Capital allocation
items.description: Company and project needs against group goals and constraints.

items.title: Future financial flexibility
items.description: The effect of today’s decision on liquidity and future opportunities.

sections.closing: The purpose is not to select a project or funding route immediately, but first to understand its relationship with the group position.

sections.heading: How does ownership structure affect financial decisions?
sections.intro: In holding and family groups, relationships between owners, companies and decision authority can affect financing and capital allocation.

items.title: Ownership structure
items.description: Relationships between owners, the parent and subsidiaries.

items.title: Decision authority
items.description: Where important capital decisions are made.

items.title: Financial relationships
items.description: Dependencies and obligations that one company’s decision may create elsewhere in the group.

sections.note: This section considers the financial implications of ownership. It does not replace legal, tax or formal corporate-governance advice.

sections.heading: Which organisations can benefit from this assessment?
sections.intro: Where several companies or activities share ownership and their decisions affect one another’s resources and obligations, a group-level initial review may be useful.

items.title: Holding companies
items.description: Groups with several subsidiaries that need to consider resources, obligations and capital programmes together.

items.title: Corporate groups
items.description: Companies or operating units connected through liquidity, financing or capital decisions.

items.title: Family business groups
items.description: Groups where family ownership, several companies and capital decisions are interrelated.

sections.heading: Where does a holding-company financial review begin?
paragraphs: The starting point does not require analysis of every company or disclosure of confidential financial documents.
The initial assessment begins with the group’s principal issue and identifies matters that may need specialist review.

items.title: Introduce the structure and issue
items.description: Describe the group, related companies and the key financial decision or concern at a high level.

items.title: Initial needs review
items.description: Consider liquidity, obligations, financing, capital allocation and company relationships.

items.title: Define an appropriate path
items.description: Where suitable, outline the specialist review and possible engagement scope.

sections.note: This stage is not preparation of consolidated statements, an audit, specialist legal or tax work, or a comprehensive group report. Scope, output and timing are agreed before specialist work begins.

sections.heading: Understand the whole group before the next capital decision
paragraphs: If questions about financing, movement of resources, obligations or investment priorities span several group companies, an initial assessment can be a useful starting point.
Once the issue is clear, an appropriate specialist path can be considered.
sections.closing: A short description is enough to begin; financial statements, contracts and confidential company information are not required at this stage.
